paras: The lynching of Estes Hairston and Lindsay was the hanging of two Black prisoners by about 150 masked men who took them from the jail at Danbury, Stokes County, North Carolina, on the night of Monday, June 20, 1881. Both had been held for months awaiting trial on charges of raping a white girl and a white woman. Wire reports said the hanging was generally approved, and a local correspondent published a defense of it.

According to the Western Sentinel of nearby Winston, Hairston was charged with raping a white girl of twelve, and Lindsay with the same offense against a white woman named Garner near Germanton. The Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic, summarizing a Daily Observer despatch, said the two had lain seven months in jail. A High Point dispatch to the Chicago Tribune added that since a lynching in Rockingham County the week before last, the two men had several times said they feared they would be lynched.

A Stokes County correspondent of the Daily Observer wrote that anger rose when both cases were continued at the last Superior Court term, a delay he attributed to counsel seeking an impartial trial. On the Sunday before the lynching, he wrote, the girl died and the woman could not be found, and people concluded that the judge would have to discharge the prisoners.

The same correspondent reported that about 150 men assembled quietly, went to the court house at midnight and "noiselessly surrounded the jail." When the jailer refused the keys, they searched for and found them, broke the cell lock with an axe and cut loose the two prisoners, who were chained together. The Tribune's dispatch told it differently, describing 150 mounted masked men who held a consultation outside the village, forced the jail doors and drove the prisoners out of town in a vehicle.

In the Tribune's account the party halted at a convenient spot, gave the prisoners a few moments to prepare, stood them in a wagon under a large oak, and drove the wagon away. The Stokes letter placed the hanging on the public road about two miles from Danbury; the Western Sentinel said about four miles from town, and the Yorkville Enquirer about three miles south.

A jury found that the two men came to their death "by hanging by parties unknown," according to the Stokes correspondent. The Tribune's dispatch said the names of the participants were not known, and no report of an arrest appears in the coverage. A Greensboro dispatch a few days later cited the Stokes County hangings while reporting new rape accusations, remarking that they did not seem to have had "the effect looked for by the lynchers."

A Danbury dispatch dated June 23 named no one and closed with the line that the punishment was "generally approved, by both white and colored people." Editors headlined it "Judge Lyoch [Lynch] Hangs Two Negroes for Outrage," "Punished." and "Meets General Approval." A Danville, Virginia, dispatch named the victims, called Lindsay "a negro boy," and reported the charge as assault on two white girls, one aged eight whose death it called "the exciting cause of the lynching."

The Chicago Tribune ran the fullest narrative under the headline "How It Is Done in North Carolina—Two Ravishers Taken from a Jail by Masked Men and Left Dangling from a Tree." Shorter items in Nevada, Wisconsin and Arkansas papers called the victims "negro ravishers" or said their "crime" was against white women, treating the charges as proven. Other briefs gave the night as Wednesday or the 22d, and one Ohio paper placed Danbury in South Carolina.

In North Carolina the Western Sentinel gave a short notice describing the men as "charged with" rape. The Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic, by contrast, reprinted the Stokes letter under the heading "Why They Were Lynched," which spoke of "the good citizens of Stokes" taking justice into their own hands.

The papers disagree on the night: the local and High Point reports said Monday, the Danville wire Tuesday, and later briefs the 22d or Wednesday. The nearer sources favor Monday, June 20, which also fits the Stokes letter's timeline of the girl's death on the preceding Sunday.
